THOUGHT: Premature infant (33 weeks) with respiratory distress beginning within hours of birth—classic timing for surfactant deficiency. Clinical signs (tachypnea 70/min, grunting, intercostal/subcostal retractions, peripheral cyanosis) indicate significant alveolar collapse and increased work of breathing. Blood gas shows hypoxemia (PaO2 60 mmHg) and respiratory acidosis (pH 7.30, PaCO2 50 mmHg), consistent with hypoventilation from low lung compliance. Chest radiograph with bilateral fine reticular/granular “ground-glass” appearance is the classic imaging pattern for neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease). Other causes (transient tachypnea of the newborn, meconium aspiration, congenital pneumonia) are less likely given prematurity, timing, and characteristic radiographic pattern. Pathophysiology: surfactant deficiency in preterm lungs leads to increased alveolar surface tension, atelectasis, V/Q mismatch, and hypoxemia.

DIAGNOSIS: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (hyaline membrane disease) due to surfactant deficiency.
